issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: Military-themed conversations are hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 51-year-old school principal; this trigger implies a combat-related context not represented anywhere else in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar People: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar
issues.explanation: Avoiding people involved in the event or who look similar fits interpersonal/assault/accident traumas better than life-threatening illness, where there are typically no 'other people involved' in that sense. It is not well supported by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'talking about the future' as a trigger is plausible, but 'alcohol smell' is hard to connect unless alcohol was part of treatment context; nothing else in the profile supports that association, making this trigger set clinically incoherent.

'People can't be trusted' is more typical of interpersonal trauma and is poorly anchored to a life-threatening illness trauma in the absence of any treatment-related betrayal, conflict, or mistrust themes elsewhere in the profile.

'Crying' is not a trauma cue but an affective response/behavior, so it is clinically incoherent as a trigger item relative to the other trigger items, which are concrete sensory reminders linked to life-threatening illness (alcohol smell, hospital/antiseptic smell).

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: A global mistrust appraisal is a poor fit for the rest of the profile and trauma type. In life-threatening illness, the other items center on altered self and self-reliance, while 'People can't be trusted' implies an interpersonal betrayal/threat theme that is not supported by the memory, trigger, or strategy items and does not align well with the otherwise weak/inactive Threat links.

vignette:
The night the aneurysm ruptured, Marcus had been sitting at his desk in the den, reviewing a budget proposal for the upcoming school year. He remembered the sudden, catastrophic pressure behind his eyes, the way his vision dissolved into a white noise of static, and the terrifying sensation of his own body becoming a trap he could not escape. He had been alone. His wife, Lena, had died three years earlier from ovarian cancer, and in that moment, as he lay on the floor unable to move his left side, he was certain he was following her. The emergency surgery saved his life, but it did not save the man he had been.

Now, fifteen months later, Marcus could not deliberately recall the details of that night. When he tried, the memory slipped away like water through his fingers, leaving only a frustrating blank. Yet the emotional weight of it would hit him without warning—a wave of pure, animal terror that surged through him in the middle of a staff meeting or while he was standing in the grocery store, with no image attached, only the feeling of his heart trying to escape his chest. Worse still were the bodily reenactments: a sudden stiffness in his left arm, a feeling that his head was being tilted back, and he would be back on that cold floor, paralyzed and waiting to die.

The world had become a landscape of traps. A whiff of hand sanitizer in the hallway at school could send him reeling, the antiseptic smell instantly conjuring the ICU. The sharp, sweet scent of alcohol from a parent’s breath at a conference made his stomach clench, a visceral reminder of the night he had been told he might not wake up. He began to dread his own annual physical, the cold stethoscope and the probing questions feeling like a prelude to another catastrophe. These triggers did not just disturb him; they confirmed a terrible new truth. He had come to believe that his own body was fundamentally unreliable, a ticking bomb he could no longer trust. The person he saw in the mirror—this hypervigilant, trembling man who flinched at a cough—was unrecognizable to him. He was certain he could not rely on himself to handle even a minor medical appointment, let alone another crisis.

In response, Marcus built a fortress of avoidance. He cut off all contact with his closest friends, cancelling dinners and ignoring calls, because every conversation felt like a minefield where someone might ask how he was doing. Before any interaction, whether with a teacher or a district superintendent, he would rehearse what he was going to say, running the script over and over in his head until it felt safe. He isolated himself completely, spending his evenings alone in his house, the silence a relief from the terror of unexpected questions. He refused to enter a hospital for any reason, even to visit a sick colleague, and he cancelled his annual physical three times. These strategies offered him a brittle sense of control, but they deepened his belief that he was a broken man. The more he isolated, the more he felt like a stranger to himself, and the more he rehearsed, the more he confirmed that he could not trust his own spontaneous responses.

The isolation also starved him of the very social support that might have helped his memory settle. Without anyone to talk to about what happened, the fragmented, terrifying intrusions grew only more powerful. Each sudden, image-less wave of panic or bodily reenactment further cemented his sense of being fundamentally damaged, a man who had lost his own autobiography. This, in turn, made him even more vigilant, scanning every room for the smell of antiseptic, every conversation for a medical reference. The cycle tightened until his world had shrunk to the size of his house, his job, and a narrow, rehearsed path between them.

What finally brought Marcus to a therapist’s office was not his own suffering, but a practical failure. During a fire drill at school, a first-grader had scraped her knee. The sight of the blood, the sudden proximity of a medical moment, sent Marcus into a full dissociative episode in front of the entire student body. He had frozen, unable to speak, his left arm stiffening as he felt himself back on that floor. The school board insisted he take a leave of absence. Sitting in the waiting room, he was terrified—not of the therapy itself, but of what it might unearth. He was most afraid that if he tried to remember that night deliberately, the memory would finally surface, and it would destroy whatever was left of him.
